judge_assessment.explanation: The first hard failure is supported. The worksheet directions state 'State the theorem you are using before you substitute', the answer key answers every problem by naming it first ('Interior Angle Sum Theorem: a convex n-gon splits into n-2 triangles...'), and verify.json holds ten entries of which nine are solve with a bare numeric expected and one (id 10) is manual. No entry records a theorem name and none of problems 1 through 9 carries a manual companion, so a response required on every objective problem is recorded on none of them. The second hard failure is literally true -- problem 7 says 'Set up the equation from the interior angle sum rather than guessing' and verify.json id 7 records expected [12] -- with one nuance the judge does not note: the entry's expr is '(n - 2)*180 - 150*n', which IS the required equation, so the equation exists in the data even though it is not declared as a checked response. That makes problem 7 the mildest instance rather than the sharpest one; problems 1 through 6, 8 and 9 have the same gap with no such consolation. All nine values recompute exactly (720, 2340, 135, 30, 93, 15, 12, 36, 13) and the problem-10 manual proof of the 360-degree exterior sum is correct and correctly keyed. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 4 does something most polygon sheets get wrong, and the key says so explicitly: 'Note that the number of sides never enters through the interior-sum formula here -- the exterior total is the same 360 degrees for every convex polygon.' Naming the non-dependence is what stops a student from carrying the (n-2)180 habit into every exterior-angle question.

The reverse-direction items are properly interleaved rather than bolted on. Problems 6, 7 and 9 each run a formula backwards from a given angle or sum to n (24n = 360, (n-2)180 = 150n, (n-2)180 = 1980), and they are separated by forward items, so the student cannot settle into one direction.

Problem 8 introduces the ratio device (angles as x, 2x, 3x, 4x summing to 360) without changing the underlying theorem, so it adds an algebraic layer to a known rule instead of adding a new rule. That is the right way to raise difficulty inside procedural fluency.

Problem 10 is honestly manual with a substantive desc that states the required argument (interior sum plus the linear pair at each vertex, general in n) rather than a bare 'explain why' -- and the worksheet stem constrains it usefully: 'Your explanation must work for a general n, not just for one example.'

root_causes.description: The theorem name required by the directions is a response with no representable form. Every verify type yields a number; `manual` is read as reserved for open reasoning, and naming a theorem from a short closed list does not feel open. With nothing to declare, the requirement stated once in the shared directions was declared on no problem, and per-id coverage was already satisfied by the numeric entry.
evidence: worksheet directions: 'State the theorem you are using before you substitute.'
answer_key.pdf: each solution opens by naming the theorem -- 'Interior Angle Sum Theorem', 'The exterior angles of any convex polygon total 360 degrees'
verify.json: ids 1-9 are single solve entries with numeric expected; id 10 is the only manual entry
SKILL.md line 189: 'every problem id 1..N has at least one check'

root_causes.description: The prompt asked for a ramp 'from a worked pattern to independent fluency, without repeating an identical problem skeleton', and problems 1 and 2 are the same skeleton with n changed: 'Find the sum of the interior angles of a convex hexagon' and 'Find the sum of the interior angles of a convex 15-gon'. Their verify entries are also structurally identical ('s - (6-2)*180' and 's - (15-2)*180'). Separately, no problem on the sheet is a worked pattern -- the modelled example lives only in the study guide, so the ramp starts at independent recall rather than at a demonstrated one.
evidence: worksheet problems 1 and 2, differing only in n
verify.json ids 1 and 2: 's - (6 - 2)*180' -> [720] and 's - (15 - 2)*180' -> [2340], both difficulty 1, both bloom 'recall'
prompt: 'Build a clean difficulty ramp from a worked pattern to independent fluency, without repeating an identical problem skeleton.'

improvements.title: The theorem name required by the directions needs a manual entry on every objective problem
improvements.proposed_change: State in SKILL.md that a required NAMED JUSTIFICATION -- theorem, postulate, rule, method -- is a response slot in its own right and takes a companion `manual` entry under the same id with the expected name in `desc`, even when the vocabulary is small and closed. Enforce it in scripts/verify.py by scanning the shared directions block and each problem segment for naming imperatives ('state the theorem', 'name the theorem', 'name the postulate', 'state which rule') and exiting 2 with the list of ids that carry no manual entry. On curr-332 that fires on ids 1 through 9, because the requirement is stated once in the directions rather than per problem -- which is exactly why it was missed.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture whose directions read 'State the theorem you are using before you substitute' and whose verify JSON contains only solve entries; assert verify.py exits 2 and lists every objective problem id. It exits 0 today because each id has a numeric check.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the manual boundary honest on a sheet that currently reports nine of ten problems fully machine-verified while half of each requested answer -- the named theorem, which is what distinguishes procedural fluency from formula recall -- is unrecorded.
improvements.risk: Medium. A directions-level scan flags every id at once, which is correct here and noisy on sheets whose directions carry an aspirational instruction. Warn-only for one run, then promote to a standing exit-2.

improvements.title: Problem 7's required equation in n is a printed response covered only incidentally
improvements.proposed_change: Count printed response slots per \problem segment in tests/check_layout.py and fail when the count exceeds the entries carrying that id, so an explicit 'set up the equation' instruction cannot be discharged by the root alone. For problem 7 the fix is cheap and improves the artifact: add a companion manual entry whose desc states the expected setup '(n-2)*180 = 150n', which is already the entry's expr, so the answer key's grading note can be generated from the same string the verifier solves.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem whose stem reads 'Set up the equation from the interior angle sum rather than guessing' with a single solve entry for its id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero naming the uncovered setup slot. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Bounded but real: the sheet asks the student to show the equation precisely because guessing n reaches 12 quickly, and today only the guessable answer is checked.
improvements.risk: Low. The expected setup is already present as the entry's expr, so the change is a desc plus a slot count, with no new mathematics to get wrong.

improvements.title: Problems 1 and 2 repeat one skeleton with only n changed
improvements.proposed_change: Rebuild problem 2 so it exercises a different move at the same difficulty -- for example give the interior sum of a hexagon as worked scaffolding in problem 1 (the 'worked pattern' the prompt asks the ramp to start from) and make problem 2 ask for one interior angle of a regular hexagon, which uses the same theorem through a division the sheet does not otherwise meet until problem 3. Generally: add a check to scripts/verify.py that flags two entries sharing a skill and difficulty whose exprs are identical after numeric literals are normalised away, as a warn-level design signal.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture verify JSON whose ids 1 and 2 hold 's - (6-2)*180' and 's - (15-2)*180' at the same skill and difficulty; assert verify.py emits the duplicate-skeleton warning. No such check exists today.
improvements.expected_impact: Honours the prompt's explicit 'without repeating an identical problem skeleton' clause, and buys back one slot on a ten-problem sheet for a genuinely different item.
improvements.risk: Low, but the normalisation must be loose enough not to flag legitimate practice pairs on a sheet declared "format": "drill"; keep it warn-level only.

case_summary: The polygon-angle mathematics is entirely correct (720, 2340, 135, 30, 93, 15, 12, 36, 13, plus a valid general proof of the 360-degree exterior sum), the reverse-direction items are well interleaved with the forward ones, and problem 4's key note that the number of sides never enters the exterior computation is exactly the misconception worth pre-empting. The rejection is right: the directions require 'State the theorem you are using before you substitute', the key names a theorem at the top of every solution, and none of the nine objective problems carries any record of that response -- verify.json holds nine bare numeric solve entries plus one manual. Problem 7 is the mildest instance rather than the sharpest, since its entry's expr '(n-2)*180 - 150*n' is the very equation the stem demands; problems 1 through 6, 8 and 9 have the same gap with nothing standing in for it. One design note beyond the judge: problems 1 and 2 are the same skeleton with n changed, which the prompt explicitly asked the sheet to avoid, and the sheet's ramp has no worked pattern on it -- the modelled example lives only in the study guide.
